question: Where can I find a fractional CRO?
body:
## Direct Answer

You can find a fractional CRO through specialized fractional-executive marketplaces (Chief Outsiders, Go Fractional, Continuum, Bolster), executive-search and RevOps consultancies, vetted operator networks like Pavilion and RevGenius, warm referrals from your VCs and board, and targeted LinkedIn sourcing. The fastest reliable path is a marketplace or operator network for pre-vetted supply, layered with two or three warm referrals so you can compare a matched candidate against people who already have someone's trust.

Hiring a fractional Chief Revenue Officer is less like posting a job and more like sourcing a specialized consultant who will sit inside your leadership team one to three days a week. The supply exists in several distinct channels, each with a different trade-off between speed, vetting depth, cost, and fit. Below is where each channel lives, how to evaluate what comes out of it, and how to run a hiring process that ends with the right operator rather than the most available one.

## What is the fastest place to find a vetted fractional CRO?

The fastest vetted route is a fractional-executive marketplace, because the vetting, contracting, and matching are already productized. Platforms such as **Chief Outsiders**, **Go Fractional**, **Continuum**, **Bolster**, and **The Fractional CxO Collective** maintain rosters of operators who have already run revenue orgs, and they match you against three to five candidates within a week or two. You describe your stage, revenue, motion (product-led, sales-led, or hybrid), and the specific gap — pipeline, pricing, sales leadership, or go-to-market strategy — and the marketplace returns a shortlist rather than an inbox full of unqualified applicants.

The trade-off is that marketplaces optimize for coverage across their roster, not for the single best operator in your niche. A marketplace match is a strong starting shortlist, not a finished decision. Treat the first three candidates as a calibration set: they teach you what "good" looks like at your price point and stage, and they surface the questions you didn't know to ask. Even teams that ultimately hire through a referral usually run a marketplace search first because it is the cheapest way to learn the market rate and the shape of available supply. For a deeper breakdown of how these engagements are scoped and priced, see the [RevOps guide to fractional leadership models](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-cro-models).

Speed on a marketplace comes from three things being pre-built that you would otherwise have to assemble yourself. First, the roster is already assembled and lightly screened, so you are not spending two weeks generating a candidate list from cold outreach. Second, the intake questionnaire forces you to articulate your stage, motion, and gap in a structured way, which means the match is against a real brief rather than a vibe — and that same clarity makes every downstream interview sharper. Third, the contracting paperwork (MSA, SOW, invoicing, sometimes payroll-of-record) is templated, so the gap between "we picked someone" and "they started work" is days rather than the weeks a bespoke legal cycle would consume. Those three compressions are exactly why the marketplace path routinely beats a self-run search on wall-clock time even when the eventual hire is comparable in quality.

The failure mode to watch on marketplaces is treating the first-returned shortlist as an endorsement of fit rather than a filter for availability and baseline credibility. The platform is optimizing partly for who is available this month and who converts, not solely for who is the sharpest operator for your precise problem. Push back on a thin shortlist: ask the platform's matcher to re-run against a tighter brief, request candidates who have specifically operated in your motion, and do not be shy about rejecting all three and asking for a second batch. A marketplace earns its fee by absorbing that iteration for you, so use it.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Start the search] --> B[Define stage motion and the gap]
  B --> C[Marketplace shortlist]
  B --> D[Warm referrals from VCs and board]
  B --> E[Operator networks]
  C --> F[Compare three to five candidates]
  D --> F
  E --> F
  F --> G[Paid trial engagement]
  G --> H[Convert to ongoing or exit clean]
```

## Where do the best fractional CRO referrals actually come from?

The highest-signal source is a warm referral from someone who has already worked with the operator. Referrals compress the vetting timeline because the reference check is baked into the introduction — the person vouching has watched the CRO close deals, build a team, or fix a broken forecast. In practice, the four richest referral wells are your **investors** (VCs place fractional revenue leaders into portfolio companies constantly and keep a mental roster), your **board and advisors**, **other founders at your stage**, and **the operators themselves**, who tend to travel in tight networks and will happily refer a peer when a role isn't their fit.

The reason referrals outperform is selection. Anyone can list themselves on a marketplace or a LinkedIn banner; far fewer get named unprompted by a founder who staked their own credibility on the introduction. When you ask a VC "who did you place at the last three portfolio companies that hit their number," you are filtering for demonstrated outcomes rather than self-description. The weakness of referrals is coverage: your network only knows the operators it knows, and those people are frequently at capacity. That is why referrals pair so well with marketplaces — the marketplace gives you breadth and a market-rate baseline, and referrals give you depth and trust. Run both in parallel and let the referred candidates set the quality bar you hold marketplace candidates to. The mechanics of these networks are covered in the [operator-network sourcing playbook](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/operator-network-sourcing).

Do not skip the reference call just because the introduction was warm. A referral tells you the operator was good in someone else's context; it does not tell you they fit yours. A CRO who was excellent scaling a 20-person enterprise sales team may be the wrong hire for a founder-led, product-led company that has never written a sales comp plan. The referral gets you a trusted candidate faster; the fit work is still yours to do.

There is also a craft to asking for referrals that most founders get wrong: they ask an open question and get a polite non-answer. "Do you know any good fractional CROs?" invites a list of names with no signal attached. The sharper ask names an outcome and a context: "Who did you see personally take a founder-led SaaS company from roughly one to three million in ARR by building an outbound motion?" That framing does two things. It forces the referrer to reach for a specific memory of results rather than a rolodex of acquaintances, and it filters for stage-and-motion match before you have spent a single call. When someone answers a question like that with immediate conviction — a name, a company, a number — you have found high signal. When they hesitate or generalize, you have learned the referral is weaker than the warmth of the introduction suggested, which is itself useful.

Finally, treat operators as a referral channel in their own right, not just as candidates. A strong fractional CRO who is at capacity or who reads your problem as a poor fit for their skills will very often name the person who *is* the right fit — and because they are staking peer reputation on it, that referral is among the highest-signal you will get. Ending every candidate conversation, even the ones that go nowhere, with "who else should I be talking to?" turns your rejected shortlist into a compounding source of better candidates.

## Which platforms and networks list fractional CROs?

There are four categories of channel, and the strongest searches touch at least three of them. First, **dedicated fractional marketplaces** — Chief Outsiders, Go Fractional, Continuum, Bolster, Toptal's executive tier, and The Fractional CxO Collective — productize matching and contracting. Second, **operator and RevOps communities** — Pavilion, RevGenius, Modern Sales Pros, and Sales Assembly — are membership networks full of senior revenue leaders, many of whom take fractional work between full-time roles; you find people there through job-board posts, member directories, and Slack channels rather than a formal match. Third, **executive-search and consulting firms** run fractional and interim placement desks; these cost more but carry deeper vetting and a replacement guarantee. Fourth, **direct sourcing on LinkedIn**, where "Fractional CRO" is now a common headline and Sales Navigator lets you filter by title, industry, and company size.

Each channel front-loads a different kind of risk. Marketplaces front-load convenience and market-rate transparency but can feel transactional. Communities front-load peer trust and are excellent for warm introductions, but you do the matching yourself, which takes time. Search firms front-load rigor and guarantees at a premium price and a slower timeline. Direct LinkedIn sourcing front-loads control and lowest cost but pushes the entire vetting burden onto you, and the volume of self-declared fractional CROs makes signal-to-noise the core challenge. The right mix depends on how much of the vetting work you want to own versus outsource, and how fast you need someone in the seat.

A practical way to sequence the channels is to run them as concentric circles rather than a single funnel. Start with the warmest, cheapest circle — your investors, board, and peer founders — because a single strong referral there can end the search before you touch a platform. In parallel, open one marketplace search to establish the market rate and a baseline shortlist, so you are never negotiating in the dark. Only if those two circles come up thin do you move outward to community sourcing (more work, more warmth) and finally to a retained search firm (most rigor, most cost, most time). Structuring it this way means you spend money and effort in proportion to how hard the search actually turns out to be, instead of committing to the most expensive channel before you know you need it.

Watch for the specialization dimension underneath the channel choice, too. A generalist fractional CRO from a broad marketplace may be exactly right if your gap is "install a repeatable sales system." But if your problem is narrow and technical — usage-based pricing for a PLG product, a channel-partner motion, a shift from SMB to enterprise, or a regulated-industry sales cycle — you often want a channel that lets you filter for that specialization directly. Niche operator communities and specialist search desks tend to out-resolve a general marketplace on those precise problems, because the match is against a named motion rather than a broad "revenue leader" label. Name your specialization requirement out loud in the brief; it changes which channel deserves your first hour.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Channel choice] --> B[Marketplaces]
  A --> C[Operator communities]
  A --> D[Search firms]
  A --> E[Direct LinkedIn]
  B --> F[Fast and market rate transparent]
  C --> G[Warm and peer vetted]
  D --> H[Rigorous and guaranteed but pricey]
  E --> I[Cheapest but you own all vetting]
```

## How do I vet a fractional CRO once I find one?

Vetting a fractional CRO is different from vetting a full-time hire because you are buying a diagnosis and a system, not a decade of tenure. The single most predictive signal is stage-and-motion match: a CRO who has taken a company from your current revenue to your next milestone, in your sales motion, in a comparable market. Ask for the specific numbers — starting ARR, ending ARR, the time it took, and what they personally changed. Vague answers about "driving growth" are a red flag; strong operators talk in pipeline coverage ratios, win rates, ramp times, and specific systems they installed.

Run a structured reference process even when the candidate came warm. Call two people who reported to them and one peer, and ask behavioral questions: what did this person actually build, what broke while they were there, and would you hire them again. Then require a **paid diagnostic engagement** before any longer commitment — two to four weeks in which the candidate audits your funnel, forecast, and team, then presents a written plan. This is the truest test available, because it reveals how they think inside your specific data rather than how they present in an interview. A great fractional CRO will scope this trial themselves and often suggest it before you do. The scoring rubric for this stage lives in the [fractional executive evaluation framework](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-cro-models), and the trial-to-conversion mechanics are covered below.

Beware three common failure modes. The **over-networked adviser** who wants to strategize but never touches the CRM or a live deal — fractional CROs must operate, not just advise. The **capacity-stretched operator** juggling six clients, where you get their leftover hours; ask directly how many active engagements they carry and cap it in the contract. And the **wrong-stage veteran** whose playbook was built at a company ten times your size and does not compress down to your reality. Each of these can look excellent in a first call, which is exactly why the paid trial matters more than the interview.

It helps to know what a strong reference call actually sounds like versus a weak one. A weak reference confirms adjectives — "she was great, really smart, the team loved her" — which tells you nothing you can act on. A strong reference produces specifics under gentle pressure: what the forecast looked like when the operator arrived and when they left, which deals they personally unstuck, which rep they coached up or moved out, and what the operator got *wrong* along the way. That last question is the most revealing, because every real operator has a scar, and a reference who can name one is describing a real working relationship rather than reciting a testimonial. If three references in a row can only offer warmth and no texture, treat that as its own signal — you are likely talking to someone whose reputation outruns their operating track record.

Give equal weight to how the candidate scopes the paid trial, because the scoping itself is a competency test. A strong operator will narrow the trial to a small number of concrete deliverables — an honest audit of pipeline hygiene, a rebuilt forecast, a written thirty-sixty-ninety plan, a read on which two reps are miscast — and will tell you what they cannot credibly deliver in four weeks. A weaker candidate will accept a vague, sprawling trial mandate and promise to "get their arms around everything," which usually produces a glossy deck and no operating traction. What you are really testing in the trial is judgment under real constraints: can this person walk into ambiguous data, find the one or two things that actually move revenue, and say so plainly? That is the job, and the trial is the only interview format that measures it directly.

## How much does a fractional CRO cost and how is the engagement structured?

Fractional CRO engagements are typically priced as a monthly retainer tied to a committed number of days per week, most commonly one to three days. Because rates vary widely by market, seniority, and scope, do not anchor on a single number you read somewhere — get live quotes from three candidates and let the spread tell you the market rate for your stage. The structure matters as much as the price: define the days per week, the specific outcomes owned, the reporting cadence, and a clean exit clause. A well-structured engagement has a defined scope (for example, "build the outbound motion and hire two AEs in ninety days") rather than an open-ended "run revenue" mandate that quietly expands.

The most common structures are a **fixed monthly retainer** for a set number of days, a **project-based engagement** with a defined deliverable and end date, and a **retainer-plus-conversion** path where the fractional engagement is explicitly a trial for a future full-time or equity role. Many founders use the fractional period precisely as an extended, paid audition for a permanent CRO — you get months of real work product before committing to a full-time salary and equity grant. Whatever the structure, insist on written monthly deliverables and a thirty-day exit so that a bad fit costs you weeks, not quarters. The contracting patterns and typical clause language are detailed in the [operator-network sourcing playbook](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/operator-network-sourcing).

When you compare quotes, compare the *unit of value*, not just the headline monthly number. A candidate charging more per day but committing to a specific outcome in a fixed window can be dramatically cheaper in true cost than a lower day-rate operator on an open-ended retainer that drifts for two extra quarters. Normalize the quotes against the deliverable: what does each candidate promise to have built, hired, or fixed by a named date, and what happens to the fee if they miss it? That reframing usually collapses a confusing spread of numbers into a clear picture of who is pricing their confidence and who is pricing their calendar.

Build the exit and the scope-creep guardrails into the contract from day one, while everyone is still optimistic, because that is the only moment you have leverage to do it cleanly. The clauses that earn their keep are: a hard cap on the operator's total concurrent clients, so you are not silently deprioritized; a monthly written deliverable requirement, so progress is legible rather than asserted; a thirty-day exit either party can trigger without cause, so a bad fit is a rounding error rather than a legal fight; and an explicit conversion path — trigger, comp band, equity treatment — if the fractional role is a runway to full-time. Writing the conversion terms early is not presumptuous; it removes the awkward renegotiation that otherwise happens exactly when the engagement is going well and both sides have the least incentive to be disciplined about it.

## When should I hire a fractional CRO instead of a full-time one?

Hire fractional when you have a revenue problem that needs senior judgment but not forty hours a week of it. The classic triggers are: a founder-led sales motion that has hit its ceiling and needs a system; a first-time push into a new segment or motion where you lack in-house expertise; a gap between a departed VP of Sales and a full-time CRO you are not ready to fund; or a board that wants professional revenue leadership before the company can justify a full executive salary and equity package. In all of these, a fractional CRO gives you the seniority immediately and lets you defer the full-time commitment until the revenue supports it.

Choose full-time instead when revenue leadership needs to be present daily — deep team management, high-velocity hiring, or a motion complex enough that part-time attention would leave deals and reps unmanaged. A useful test: if the core need is **building a system and installing playbooks**, fractional fits, because systems can be designed in concentrated days and then run by the team. If the core need is **being in the room for every deal and every rep every day**, you need full-time. Many companies sequence the two deliberately — a fractional CRO builds the revenue engine and hires the team over six to nine months, then either converts to full-time or hands off to a permanent hire they helped recruit. That sequencing is often the cheapest path to durable revenue leadership, and it turns the search itself into the first deliverable.

There is a cost-and-risk logic underneath the choice that is worth making explicit. A full-time CRO is a large fixed cost — salary, equity, benefits, and the significant expense and disruption of a mis-hire that takes months to surface and quarters to unwind. A fractional CRO converts that fixed cost into a variable one you can size to the problem and exit in thirty days. For a company that is still discovering what its revenue motion even is, that optionality is worth a great deal: you are buying senior judgment *and* the ability to be wrong cheaply. The full-time hire makes sense once the motion is known and the constraint is throughput of leadership attention rather than clarity about direction.

Watch for the signals that it is time to convert or graduate out of the fractional arrangement, because staying fractional too long has its own cost. When the revenue engine the operator built now needs daily stewardship — a growing team that requires real management, a deal volume that outpaces two or three days a week, a board that wants a single accountable owner in every meeting — the part-time structure starts to bottleneck the very growth it created. The cleanest outcomes usually run in one of two directions: the fractional operator converts to full-time on pre-agreed terms, or they run the search for their own full-time replacement and hand off a documented, working system. Either way, the fractional period will have paid for itself twice — once in the engine it built, and again in de-risking the permanent hire that follows.

## Related questions

### What is the difference between a fractional CRO and a sales consultant?
A fractional CRO owns revenue outcomes and operates inside your leadership team with decision authority; a consultant advises and hands off recommendations. The CRO builds and runs; the consultant diagnoses and departs.

### Can a fractional CRO become full-time?
Yes, and many engagements are structured as an extended paid audition. Founders commonly convert a strong fractional operator to full-time once revenue justifies the salary and equity, using the trial period as de-risked evidence.

### How many days a week does a fractional CRO work?
Typically one to three days per week per client, set in the contract. Ask how many total clients they carry so you know your realistic share of their attention.

### Do fractional CROs take equity?
Sometimes, especially when a conversion to full-time is on the table or cash is tight. Equity is more common in retainer-plus-conversion structures than in pure project engagements.

### Where do VCs find fractional CROs for their portfolio companies?
Through their own operator networks, prior portfolio placements, and dedicated marketplaces. Asking your investors directly is one of the highest-signal referral sources available to you.

### What size company typically hires a fractional CRO?
Most often early to growth-stage companies past initial product-market fit that need senior revenue leadership before they can justify a full-time executive package. The fit narrows once a large team needs daily management.

## FAQ

**Where is the single best place to start looking?**
Start with a fractional-executive marketplace to get a fast, vetted shortlist and a market-rate baseline, then run two or three warm referrals in parallel to pressure-test the marketplace candidates against people who already have someone's trust.

**How long does it take to hire a fractional CRO?**
A marketplace shortlist typically arrives within one to two weeks, and with a paid diagnostic trial you can go from search to a working engagement in three to five weeks — far faster than the multi-month timeline of a full-time executive search.

**How do I vet a fractional CRO quickly?**
Match them on stage and sales motion, run three structured reference calls including two former direct reports, and require a two-to-four-week paid diagnostic engagement before any longer commitment. The trial reveals how they think inside your data.

**Is LinkedIn a good place to find one?**
Yes for control and cost, but it pushes all vetting onto you. Use Sales Navigator to filter by title, industry, and company size, and expect to do heavier reference work because anyone can add "Fractional CRO" to their headline.

**Should I use a search firm?**
Use one when you want deep vetting and a replacement guarantee and are willing to pay a premium and wait longer. For most early and growth-stage companies, a marketplace plus referrals delivers comparable quality faster and cheaper.

**What should the contract include?**
Days per week, specific outcomes owned, monthly written deliverables, a reporting cadence, a cap on the operator's total concurrent clients, and a thirty-day exit clause so a bad fit costs weeks rather than quarters.

**How do I know if I need fractional versus full-time?**
If the core need is building systems and playbooks that the team then runs, fractional fits. If revenue leadership must be present daily for every deal and every rep, hire full-time.

**Can operator communities like Pavilion help?**
Yes. Pavilion, RevGenius, and similar networks are full of senior revenue leaders who take fractional work between roles. You find them through member directories, job boards, and Slack channels, and referrals through these communities carry strong peer trust.

**What questions should I ask in the first call?**
Ask for a specific before-and-after: starting ARR, ending ARR, the timeline, and exactly what they personally changed. Ask how many clients they currently carry, and ask what they got wrong at their last engagement. Concrete answers signal a real operator; adjectives signal a presenter.

**How do I compare quotes from different candidates?**
Compare the unit of value, not the headline number. Normalize each quote against the deliverable and the deadline — a higher day-rate tied to a committed outcome often costs less in total than a cheaper open-ended retainer that drifts for extra quarters.
